title: Infra: GPU fleet, capacity, networking, IaC & CI/CD playbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's standards and runbooks for operating the GPU fleet and associated infra: capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD build pipelines, and day-2 runbooks. It is intended for infra, SRE, and serving-runtime engineers responsible for provisioning, running, and scaling inference capacity.

Goals and scope
- Provide a single source of truth for GPU fleet sizing, autoscaling, and allocation policies.
- Standardize Terraform/IaC module patterns and naming conventions used across GPU fleets, VPCs, and shared networking.
- Define CI/CD pipeline requirements for infra changes (plan/validate/apply) and build artifacts for runtime images.
- Provide operational runbooks for capacity incidents, network failures, and rollout/rollback procedures.

Audience and ownership
- Primary audience: eng-infra, eng-serving-runtime, eng-sre.
- Document owner_team: engineering (infra).
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any cloud/network/GPU SKU change.

Table of contents (this document)
1. Ownership & SLAs
2. GPU fleet capacity model and policy
3. Cloud accounts & networking patterns
4. Terraform/IaC modules and guidelines
5. CI/CD and build pipeline standards
6. Runbooks (incidents & operational procedures)
7. Day-2 operations and playbook links
8. Appendices: examples and CLI snippets

1) Ownership & SLAs
- Service owner: infra-gpu-team (primary). On-call: infra-sre rotation for capacity incidents.
- SLOs: control-plane provisioning latency (95th percentile) <= 5 minutes for small pod allocations; node replacement MTTR <= 15 minutes (hardware/driver faults).
- Utilization targets: target steady-state GPU utilization = 30-55% (workload-dependent). Maintain headroom so that p95 latency SLOs are met under burst demand.
- Emergency contacts: pager for infra-sre (escalation path in oncall playbook).

2) GPU fleet capacity model and policy
Overview
- We operate mixed GPU SKUs (A100-40GB, A100-80GB, H100 where available) across clouds/regions. Fleet capacity is modeled at the pod-level and node-level.
- Two logical pools: Dedicated (reserved for enterprise customers) and Shared (hosted/public workloads). Each pool has separate capacity planning and quota rules.

Capacity planning terms
- Provisioned capacity: raw GPUs attached to nodes.
- Allocatable capacity: capacity available to the scheduler after overhead (driver, kube-reserved).
- Committed baseline: conservative minimum capacity to support committed SLAs for Dedicated customers.
- Buffer pool: on-demand buffer (uncommitted) to absorb bursts (target 10-20% of peak expected load).

Sizing guidelines
- Target headroom: maintain 20% headroom above expected 99th percentile token-per-second demand for autoscale responsiveness.
- Scale unit: scale in/out at node granularity. Prefer smaller node sizes if low-latency autoscaling is critical; prefer larger units (multi-GPU) for cost efficiency for background/batch workloads.
- Preferred instance types: list labels are illustrative: ["gcp-a2-highgpu-1g", "gcp-a2-highgpu-2g", "aws-p4d.24xlarge (H100-equivalent)", "azure-ncav4 (A100)"]

Allocation policies
- Dedicated pool: capacity reserved via monthly/annual commits. Enforce strict quota checks via account-level IAM and Terraform-managed tags.
- Shared pool: fairness policy based on weighted tokens; burst allowed up to buffer pool subject to preemption.
- Preemption: preemptible/spot nodes can be used for non-latency critical workloads with automated graceful eviction hooks.

Autoscaling & orchestration
- Two-layer scaling model: (1) Scheduler-level autoscaler (Karpenter/HPA) for pods, (2) Cluster autoscaler (cloud autoscaler/cluster-autoscaler or custom controller) for nodes.
- Warm pools: keep a small warm pool of nodes (5-10% of baseline) to reduce provisioning latency for common SKUs.
- Scale cooldown: avoid oscillation by setting 1-2 minute minimal cool-down for pod-triggered actions and 5-10 minute cooldown for node scale events.

Metrics & alerts (examples)
- GPU utilization (per-cluster, per-pool): alert if 5m average > 85% for > 10m.
- Pending pods waiting for GPU: alert if >10 for >5m.
- Node provisioning failures: count > 3 in 10m -> page infra-sre.
- Preemption churn: > 5% of nodes churn in 10m -> investigate spot instability.

3) Cloud accounts & networking patterns
Principles
- Account isolation: Dedicated customers get separate cloud accounts/projects where required; infra shared services live in central infra accounts.
- Least privilege: all service identities follow least-privilege IAM policies. Network egress/data paths are reviewed per compliance requirements.

VPC design (recommended)
- Per-region infra VPC per account. Subnets per availability zone.
- Subnet types: private-worker-subnet, control-plane-subnet, management-subnet (bastion/jenkins).
- Shared services sit in a central services VPC with VPC peering / Transit Gateway for multi-account access.

Network security
- Security groups (SGs)/NACLs: allow only required ports (SSH from bastion), kubelet control plane ports, and monitoring/tracing endpoints.
- Private egress: NAT gateways for worker subnets; restrict direct internet egress for datasets and model weights; use controlled S3/GCS access endpoints.
- Service endpoints: use VPC endpoints for cloud storage and KMS where possible to avoid crossing public internet.

Peering & multi-account access patterns
- Use centralized Transit Gateway (AWS) or VPC peering (GCP Shared VPC) for cross-account access.
- For Dedicated accounts, route model artifact pulls through a controlled artifact-replication pipeline to avoid cross-account read over public networks.

IAM & service identities
- Use short-lived tokens where possible and workload identity federation (OIDC) for pods.
- Create dedicated roles for cluster lifecycle operations: cluster-admin-infra, node-provisioner, image-builder.

4) Terraform/IaC modules and guidelines
Top-level guidance
- All infra changes must be expressed as Terraform modules stored in the monorepo infra/modules and applied through the canonical CI/CD pipeline. Changes to shared modules require owners\u2019 review and a staged rollout.
- Keep modules small and composable: network, vpc, subnet, bastion, gpu-node-group, kms, artifact-replication.
- State management: use Terraform Cloud (or remote backend with locking) per account/region. Do not store state locally.

Module naming conventions
- Module path: modules/<domain>/<resource> (e.g., modules/gpu/node-group).
- Resource names: <env>-<region>-<service>-<resource> (e.g., prod-us-west1-inference-nodepool).

Mandatory module attributes
- owner (string): oncall rotation or team name.
- cost_center (string) for chargeback.
- tags (map/string) with standards: team, purpose, environment, customer (if dedicated).

Terraform example: gpu node group (example snippet)
```
module "gpu_node_group" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//modules/gpu/node-group?ref=v1.3.0"
  name_prefix = "prod-us-west1-inference"
  instance_type = "gcp-a2-highgpu-1g"
  gpu_count_per_node = 1
  min_size = 2
  max_size = 40
  node_labels = {
    pool = "shared-inference"
  }
  tags = {
    team = "infra-gpu"
    cost_center = "serving-runtime"
  }
}
```
Module review & rollout policy
- Changes to modules require at least two approvers from owners + a successful plan in CI.
- Rollout: apply to a staging account first, smoke-test with synthetic load, then promote to prod with canary increases.

Security & secrets
- Secrets: store KMS keys in customer-specific KMS/HSM where required. Credentials for modules delivered via workspace variables in Terraform Cloud or Vault dynamic secrets.

5) CI/CD and build pipeline standards
Principles
- All infra PRs must run plan and static checks; no direct pushes to main for infra modules.
- Pipeline must be idempotent and produce an explicit plan artifact that is stored and referenced during approvals.

Pipeline stages (recommended GitHub Actions example)
1. lint (tflint, terraform fmt check)
2. init (terraform init using remote backend credentials)
3. validate (terraform validate)
4. plan (generate plan file and upload as artifact)
5. policy-check (OPA/Conftest against company policies: e.g., disallow public subnets for worker pools)
6. manual approval (for changes affecting prod)
7. apply (run terraform apply in remote workspace or invoke Terraform Cloud run)

Sample GitHub Actions job snippet (illustrative)
```
name: tf-plan-apply
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v1
      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init -backend-config="workspace=${{ matrix.workspace }}"
      - name: Terraform Plan
        run: terraform plan -out=tfplan.binary
      - name: Upload Plan
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: tfplan.binary
```
Build artifacts and images
- Image builds for runtime containers should be reproducible and we keep signed tags. Images are built in a separate pipeline that runs unit tests, integration smoke tests, and pushing to a private registry.

Gating rules
- No infra apply to prod without: successful plan, two approvers (one must be module owner), passing policy-checks, and an integration smoke test in a staging environment.

6) Runbooks (incidents & operational procedures)
High level triage process (capacity incident)
1. Detect: alert fires (pending pods > 10 or cluster utilization > 85%).
2. Triage: oncall checks dashboard (Grafana) -> determine whether this is demand spike, provisioning failure, or misconfiguration.
3. Immediate mitigation (ordered):
   a. If provisioning failure: check cloud console for quota limits, provisioning errors, ASG/instance group errors. Execute node-group recreate if needed.
   b. If demand spike: increase buffer pool / temporarily relax quota for shared pool if safe; contact product owner for dedicated traffic.
   c. If scheduling constraints: inspect taints/tolerations and GPU resource requests; consider temporarily relaxing constraints or moving low-priority jobs to spot nodes.
4. Post-incident: open a postmortem (link template in oncall playbook) and schedule follow-up actions.

Critical commands & queries
- Check pending pods: kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o wide
- List GPU nodes: kubectl get nodes -l node.kubernetes.io/gpu=true -o wide
- Check node events: kubectl describe node <node-name>
- Trigger nodegroup scale: terraform apply -target=module.gpu_node_group -var='desired_capacity=10' (use only in emergencies and notify owners)

Incident: node hardware/driver failure
1. Detect: node exporter / node metric shows GPU health failing or kubelet not ready.
2. Immediate: cordon node (kubectl cordon <node>), drain non-critical pods with --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data, and reprovision node via autoscaler.
3. Verify: ensure pods reschedule and latency metrics return to normal.
4. Replace: file cloud provider ticket if hardware persistent; update driver image and run node-level diagnostic scripts.

Network incident runbook (egress blocked)
1. Identify impacted accounts and regions via monitoring dashboards.
2. Validate route tables and NAT gateways; check recent Terraform changes in pipelines.
3. If change caused issue: revert apply to last good state using stored plan artifact or run terraform apply against last known good workspace.

7) Day-2 operations and playbook links
- Weekly checks: verify warm pool sizes, pending pods, and preemption rates.
- Monthly: review instance-type pricing changes and re-evaluate preferred SKUs.
- Quarterly: capacity forecast refresh and Dedicated capacity negotiation review for enterprise customers.

Runbook & wiki links (canonical)
- GPU capacity & infra runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026.json
- Modules index: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/infra-iac-modules-ci-cd-guidelines-2026.json
- Incident process & postmortem template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortem-template.json

8) Appendices
A. Terraform & kubectl quick reference
- terraform plan: terraform plan -out=tfplan.binary
- terraform apply (remote): tfc run or terraform apply tfplan.binary (only in non-prod where remote backend allows).
- kubectl drain example: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force

B. Example capacity math (simplified)
- Workload A: median token/sec 1000, 99th percentile token/sec 3000. Avg tokens per GPU-second = 50. Expected 99th ptps = 3000 / 50 = 60 GPU-seconds -> map to nodes depending on gpu_count_per_node. Add 20% headroom -> 72 GPU-seconds -> choose node sizes accordingly.

C. Change log
- 2024-09-15: initial draft created (Asha Patel).
- 2025-06-02: updated autoscaling guidance and warm pool policy (Miguel Santos).
- 2026-02-20: added H100 guidance and CI/CD gating rules (Priya Raman).

If you are making changes to this playbook
- Edit the modules and run through the staging pipeline. Update related_pages and reviewers. Tag your PR with the label "infra-gpu" and notify the infra-sre oncall.

End of document
